The Talmud. A vast body of Jewish law, theology, and commentary compiled over centuries, consisting of the Mishnah from the third century CE and the Gemara from the fifth to sixth centuries CE. It serves as the primary source of rabbinic Judaism and shapes Jewish ethics, law, and practice to this day.

The Mishnah, meaning repetition, is a concise legal code organized into six orders covering ritual, agriculture, family law, damages, holy things, and purity. The Gemara, meaning completion, is expansive rabbinic discussion and interpretation of the Mishnah. It often includes debates between named scholars across generations, presenting conflicting opinions and interpretations.

Two versions exist: the Palestinian Talmud, compiled in the Land of Israel around 400 CE, and the Babylonian Talmud, compiled in Babylon around 500 CE. The Babylonian Talmud is longer and more authoritative in mainstream Judaism. The text is written in a mixture of Hebrew in the Mishnah and Aramaic in the Gemara, reflecting the linguistic reality of Jewish communities in antiquity.

The Talmud extends and interprets the Torah, addressing questions the written law leaves unanswered and applying ancient principles to new circumstances. It is famous for its dialectical style. Pages present conflicting opinions, often without final resolution, encouraging ongoing interpretation and debate. The tradition of study itself becomes a form of worship. This approach, called chavruta, involves students memorizing and debating together.

The Talmud encompasses far more than law. It includes folklore, science, medicine, ethics, and mystical teachings known as Kabbalah. The Torah, the five books of Moses, forms the foundation on which the Talmud builds. Moses, the lawgiver, is the figure whose Torah the Talmud interprets and applies. The Talmud stands central to Jewish theology, practice, and identity following the Second Temple period, serving as the primary text through which Jewish law and thought continue to develop.
